definition.text: Payments offered to farmers or landowners in return for managing their land so that it provides an ecological service.

facts.text: One definition calls PES a transparent system for the additional provision of environmental services through conditional payments to voluntary providers.
The 'big three' services drawing most money are climate change mitigation, watershed services and biodiversity conservation.
The provider usually holds property rights over the land, and receives compensation from those who benefit from its services.
Beneficiaries should pay less than their welfare gain, and providers should accept more than their cost of supplying the service.
Most PES programmes are funded by governments and run through intermediaries such as NGOs, rather than direct buyer-seller contracts.
PES is promoted as a rural development tool, though programmes are usually not designed mainly to reduce poverty.
National set-aside style PES programmes exist in Canada, the EU, Japan and Switzerland as well as the US and China.

title: Theoretical perspectives on PES

definition.text: The three main ways of viewing PES: environmental economics, ecological economics, and the rejection of ecosystem services altogether.

facts.text: Environmental economics sees PES as a voluntary, conditional deal between a service buyer and seller, rooted in the Coase theorem.
In reality transaction costs are almost always present, future payment promises are not time consistent, and financing often runs short.
Ecological economics treats natural and manufactured capital as complements, and judges PES by the weight of the incentive, how direct the transfer is, and how far the service is commodified.
Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard.
Critics argue nature should be valued for its own sake and that market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people.
Pragmatists accept the problems of valuing nature but argue that in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'.

contested_note: Environmental and ecological economists disagree on how to frame PES, and some reject valuing ecosystem services at all.

definition.text: Costa Rica's Pagos por servicios ambientales, set up in 1997 as the first PES programme run on a national scale.

facts.text: It pays for four services: greenhouse gas mitigation, water services, biodiversity protection and scenic beauty.
It was funded at first partly by a fuel tax, with a water tariff added in 2006.
By the end of 2005 its contracts covered 10% of the country, and it is estimated to have prevented 11 million tons of carbon emissions from 1999 to 2005.
Its flat-rate payment leaves many high-value areas unenrolled because their opportunity costs are higher than the payment.

definition.text: A negotiated deal in which the Vittel mineral-water brand paid nearby farmers to adopt practices that protect its groundwater.

facts.text: Intensifying farming from the 1970s raised nitrate levels in the aquifer, threatening the brand.
The pollution came from many diffuse sources, so no single farmer's share could be measured.
The company bought some land and gave technical support and time-limited payments, making it perhaps the world's best-known PES built on direct negotiation.
It is seen as a case of Coasean bargaining, though community grievances and possible overuse of water remain controversial.

title: Hoima and Kibaale PES trial
article: Payment for ecosystem services#Hoima and Kibaale, Uganda

definition.text: A 2010 to 2013 PES scheme in Uganda that was the first set up as a randomized controlled trial to measure its effect on deforestation.

facts.text: Forest owners were paid $28 per hectare per year for two years for keeping forest intact, about 5% of typical annual income.
Deforestation was 2 to 5% in participating villages against 7 to 10% in control villages.
The scheme ended after the evaluation, and old forest practices are assumed to resume once payments stop.

definition.text: A US Department of Agriculture programme that pays farmers to take cropland out of production and plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips.

facts.text: Its aims are to reduce erosion, improve water quality and benefit wildlife.
It grew out of the 1950s Soil Bank and was formally set up by the 1985 Farm Bill with 10 to 15 year contracts.
Payments are rental payments, cost-share of up to 50% of establishing cover, and extra incentives.
Money limits enrolment, so only the most qualified land receives payments.
By December 1, 2015, it had prevented more than 9 billion tons of soil from eroding.
In 2007 it was estimated to have kept 278 million pounds of nitrogen and 59 million pounds of phosphorus from leaving fields.
Ducks in the Prairie Pothole Region rose 30 percent after 1992 with its help.

definition.text: A mechanism that gives landowners and land managers incentives to look after the environment.

facts.text: England runs such schemes under Environmental Stewardship, administered by Natural England.
After leaving the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, the British government started its Environmental Land Management scheme in 2024.
Since 1998 Switzerland has tied farm subsidies to good environmental practice, such as keeping at least 7% of farmland as ecological compensation areas.

definition.text: A Chinese programme launched in 1999 that pays farmers to convert erosion-prone farmland back to vegetation to curb flooding and soil erosion.

facts.text: It is an example of payment for ecosystem services, offering farmers grain for not farming forested slopes.
It cost $43 billion by one account, with some sources citing $95 billion for the whole programme.
It has involved 124 million people in 1,897 counties in 25 provinces.
By 2010 around 15 million hectares of farmland and 17 million hectares of barren land had returned to natural vegetation.
It has generally been economically positive and has reduced erosion and flooding.
Many plantings were cheap monocultures that did little for biodiversity, though mixed forests could help at little extra cost.
